Lord's Prayer, The
LORDZ PRAYR
n. phrase (liturgical and doctrinal; the model prayer given by Christ, Matthew 6:9–13)
Prayer from Old French preiere, Medieval Latin precaria, from precari (to beseech, entreat). Lord from Old English hlāford (bread-guardian, master). The title “Lord's Prayer” is traditional rather than scriptural — the prayer belongs to the disciples as a gift from their Lord. Luke 11:1 records the disciples' request: “Lord, teach us to pray,” establishing that Jesus gave this prayer as a structured model for covenant approach to the Father, not a rote formula to exhaust the subject.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The prayer Jesus delivered to His disciples in Matthew 6:9–13 — and in briefer form in Luke 11:2–4 — stands as the normative structure of Christian prayer in the New Testament. Given in the context of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus contrasts the hypocrite's public prayer and the pagan's vain repetition before presenting His pattern: hallowing the divine name, seeking the coming of God's kingdom, submitting to the divine will on earth as in heaven, asking for daily provision, seeking forgiveness on the pattern of one's own forgiving, asking for preservation from temptation, and seeking deliverance from the evil one. The doxology — “For Yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen” — appears in the Textus Receptus and Majority Text manuscripts and in the Didache tradition, closing the prayer in ascription of divine majesty. Reformed theology reads the Lord's Prayer not as a mandatory verbal formula to be recited and exhausted but as a structural framework for all Christian petition: God's honor first, then the coming of His reign, then submission of will, then subordinated human need. Calvin in the Institutes (III.20) called it the summary of all lawful prayer. The Westminster Shorter Catechism devotes Questions 98–107 to its exposition. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.3) cites it as the form “directed by our Lord.” Its descending order from divine glory to human need rebukes every selfish or presumptuous prayer.

Webster 1828 Definition

The pattern prayer given by Christ in Matthew 6:9–13 as the structural framework for Christian petition; Reformed theology reads it not as a mandatory verbal formula but as the ordered covenant approach to God — honor first, kingdom second, need third.

LORD'S PRAYER, n. The prayer given by Jesus Christ to His disciples in Matthew 6:9–13 and Luke 11:2–4, prescribed as the model of Christian approach to God the Father. The prayer opens with hallowing of the divine name and progresses through kingdom, will, provision, forgiveness, temptation, and deliverance — a descending order from glory to human need that frames all proper Christian petition.

The Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q. 98–107) expounds each petition serially, making the Lord's Prayer the skeleton of catechetical instruction in prayer across Reformed and Presbyterian churches. Calvin's Institutes (III.20) treats it as the summary of all lawful petition, from which no genuinely Christian prayer may depart.

Reformed theology distinguishes the Lord's Prayer as a frame, not merely a formula. It may be used verbatim in corporate worship — and the Regulative Principle supports its liturgical use — but its primary function is structural: every Christian prayer should contain hallowing of the divine name, kingdom-seeking, submission of will, and honest petition for covenantal need.

The doxology (“For Yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen”) appears in the Textus Receptus and Majority Text traditions and is cited in the Didache (c. AD 100) as the form used thrice daily in early church worship. It is omitted in the Alexandrian critical text but retained in Reformed and Baptist liturgical practice on the strength of the manuscript tradition.

The petition “forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” stands as an eschatological warning: the one who has truly received divine forgiveness will be found forgiving others; the unforgiving man reveals no evidence of having received forgiveness at all (Matthew 6:14–15). This link between received and rendered forgiveness is not synergism but covenant pattern.

Key Scripture

Matthew 6:9 — "Pray, then, in this way: 'Our Father who is in heaven, hallowed be Your name."

Matthew 6:10 — "Your kingdom come. Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven."

Matthew 6:12 — "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors."

Matthew 6:13 — "And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil. (For Yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen.)'"

Modern Corruption

Modern liturgical revisionism alters the Lord's Prayer's address from “Our Father” to gender-neutral or maternal language — an assault on the Trinitarian grammar of Christ's own prayer — while the prosperity gospel strips the submission petitions to manufacture a demand-formula.

expand to see more

Feminist and progressive liturgists in mainline Protestant denominations and Roman Catholic circles have substituted “Our Mother” or “Our Father-Mother” for the opening address, following the agenda of inclusive-language liturgy promoted by figures such as Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza and the National Council of Churches' 1983 An Inclusive Language Lectionary. This is not a translation variant; it is a doctrinal amendment. Jesus addressed God as Father — the distinctive Trinitarian address of the Son to the First Person — and no creaturely authority may revise that address. The progressive claim that “Father” is merely a cultural metaphor denies the Nicene Creed's “Father Almighty” and the entire Trinitarian grammar the prayer assumes.

The evangelical prosperity-gospel tradition has weaponized “Give us this day our daily bread” as a platform for wealth-and-health demands, while silently excising the submission petition “Your will be done.” The sequence of the prayer rebukes this reading: God's glory, His kingdom, His will — three petitions upward before the bread petition descends. The Puritan reading (Owen, Ames, Perkins) correctly reads “daily bread” as modest covenantal provision — neither poverty nor excess — governed by the submission already expressed. A prayer that demands wealth while omitting submission is not the Lord's Prayer; it is self-petition with a theological veneer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Lord's Prayer draws on Kaddish covenant-address structures, Second Temple synagogue prayer patterns, and the Shema, transforming them through the unique Father-Son Trinitarian relation and the eschatological inaugurated-kingdom framework of Jesus' ministry.

expand to see more

Kaddish (Aramaic synagogue prayer) — the ancient Kaddish opens with hallowing of the divine name and prayer for the coming of God's kingdom; the structural parallel to Matthew 6:9–10 is so close that the Lord's Prayer is best read as Jesus' covenant reconstitution of this liturgical form, transformed through the Son's distinctive address to the Father.

Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–9) — Israel's covenant-address foundation; Jesus' “Our Father who is in heaven” grounds all petition in covenant relationship established by grace, not Deistic distance or merely formal religion.

Didache (c. AD 100) — prescribes the Lord's Prayer with the doxological ending and directs it be prayed three times daily; the Didache form is the strongest early evidence for the doxology's currency in first-generation church worship.

Calvin's Institutes III.20 — the most systematic Reformed treatment; Calvin reads each petition as a theological locus and establishes the prayer's structural priority over all other prayer forms in Christian piety.

Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 98–107 — nine questions expositing the Lord's Prayer petition by petition; the standard catechetical framework for prayer instruction in Reformed and Presbyterian churches.

Usage

"The Lord's Prayer's descending structure — glory to God, then kingdom, then will, then need — reorders every selfish prayer: it begins with who God is, not with what the petitioner wants, and every subsequent petition is constrained by that prior submission."

"The petition “forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” is covenantal, not synergistic: the one who has genuinely received divine forgiveness will be found forgiving others; the unforgiving petitioner reveals he has never truly received what he claims to seek."

"Pastors who teach the Lord's Prayer merely as a liturgical recitation miss its catechetical function: Calvin called it the summary of all lawful prayer, meaning its structure teaches the believer what to want, in what order, and on what covenantal ground."
